newsitem.title: CHINA: HK to deport China children despite challenges.
newsitem.headline: HK to deport China children despite challenges.

text.p: Hong Kong will press on with plans to deport children who illegally enter the special region of China despite a flurry of court challenges by distraught parents, the government said on Saturday.
"The message I want to send is that we will be firm on our repatriation action," Regina Yip, the director of immigration, told Hong Kong radio.
More than 190 mainland-born children have applied for legal aid to challenge the repatriation law, which was passed by a new Beijing-appointed legislature last week.
The law requires children, even if they have right of abode in Hong Kong, to return to China for the appropriate immigration documents. The process can take years.
Hong Kong's determination to deport the children was echoed by Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa, who is facing his first major test over the emotive immigration issue.

"On the one hand it's a humanitarian consideration," Tung said. "On the other hand there is a question whether the community as a whole, from the point of view of education, housing, medicine, social welfare -- how can we look after them and everybody else?
"We must do what is in the long-term interest of the community as a whole," he said on Saturday after returning from a visit to Beijing.
Tung said the legal challenges are proof Hong Kong is a free society where citizens can take the government to court, but he hoped the cases would fail.
Hong Kong officials fear a flood of illegal immigrants unless they return the children to China to apply for proper entry papers.
Yip said the law was clear and lawyers would be wasting their time in looking for technicalities to prevent clients from being kicked out.
"Illegal entrants will be repatriated so there is no point in exploring any loophole in our laws to encourage any children to come, hoping that they would not be sent back," Yip said.
Children who have one Hong Kong parent have residency rights under the Basic Law, a mini-constitution which came into effect on July 1.
It is estimated that 66,000 children of "separated families" are waiting in China to join parents in Hong Kong.
The families often turn to smugglers to sneak the children into Hong Kong or face demands for bribes by Chinese officials who process their papers.
Social activists and legal experts have condemned the new law as unconstitutional because it retroactively restricts rights conferred by the Basic Law.
On July 1, British colonial rule ended and Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, with its super-capitalist ways protected for 50 years.
